display: Henrik, a visiting ethnomusicology PhD student from the University of Bergen, based in Taiyuan until May. I record work songs and ritual songs from Shanxi's coal towns and what happens to singing after the mines close.

signals.text: I'm looking for elder singers in Zuoquan who learned kaihua-diao in the village before the 1980s, not the stage versions.
I'm going to Zuoquan on 6 October by the early bus and would love an introduction to any old singer there before I go.
The two folk troupe managers I met in Zuoquan only offered polished performers and said old people are 'not good to record'. I need another way in.
I want unpolished voices of old people, not performers. Stage kaihua-diao is smoothed and shortened, and the older versions have long ornaments and stretched rhythms nobody has written down.
Nobody has yet shown me what a village singer does when no troupe is involved: who they sing to, when, and for whom.
People go quiet when they see my recorder. I'd like a trusted local to be with me the first time, so the machine isn't the first thing a singer meets.
My Mandarin is around HSK 4 and rural dialects lose me. I could use someone who understands Zuoquan or Yangquan speech and could come along on field days.
The third-year grant renewal needs concrete outcomes, ideally an archive of recordings from elderly singers.
I'm also working in Jincheng, Yangquan and Datong and want to hear from people who know mining chants, hauling songs or courtship songs there.
I'm worried I'll have no new fieldwork to show if I can't find even one elder singer in Zuoquan by December. My supervisor says I have time, but I don't feel it.
I miss Bergen's rain. Taiyuan is dry and smells of coal dust, and I'm homesick for it more than I tell people.
I spent the National Day holiday alone in Taiyuan while everyone else went home.
I'm learning knife-cut noodles from a neighbour and mine come out as thick as pencils. I'd like more people to practise Mandarin and cooking with.
I transcribed a Shanxi folk lullaby by ear after hearing it ten times and want to hear more lullabies and everyday songs.

offers.text: I have a Zoom F3 field recorder, lavalier mics, a shotgun mic and a wind-shield kit, and I record clean field audio of voices in homes and outdoors.
I can pay informant honoraria from my research budget, a modest amount per session.
I have University of Bergen ethics approval for fieldwork in Shanxi, and I record only with informed consent. I can explain to families exactly how a recording will be used.
I can transcribe melodies by ear and write up ornament and rhythm details for songs that have never been notated.
I have contacts at the Shanxi University music department and the Taiyuan folklore bureau, and I can introduce researchers or local culture workers to them when it fits.
I can offer English and basic Norwegian conversation practice, and a language exchange with learners of either.
I can share my method for documenting who sang what, to whom and when, with anyone studying other communities in transition.
I have a small Taiyuan flat with a good rice cooker and a bicycle, and I can host a simple meal or a listening session.

catchers.hypo: I come from a village near Zuoquan. My grandmother is in her eighties and still sings the old kaihua-diao she learned as a girl, with no accordion or costume.
catchers.can: I can visit with a local companion, explain the research and ethics in plain terms, record only with her consent and her family's agreement, and pay a standard honorarium.
catchers.confirm: Did this person learn the songs in the village before about 1980 and is she willing to sing for a visiting researcher?

catchers.hypo: I work at a township cultural station in Yangquan and know several retired miners who used to sing hauling songs underground.
catchers.can: I can come to Yangquan, record the singers with their consent, and share copies and credit with the station.
catchers.confirm: Do you know specific retired miners who still sing the old songs and would agree to be recorded?

catchers.hypo: I'm a university student from Zuoquan and speak the local dialect. I'd go with a foreign researcher on weekends to talk with old people.
catchers.can: I can pay a day rate for interpreting within my budget, give you credit in the work, and teach you about recording and consent.
catchers.confirm: Do you speak the Zuoquan dialect well enough to follow an old villager, and are you free on weekends from now until December?

catchers.hypo: My father taped coal-town singers on cassettes in the 1980s and the tapes are still in a drawer. I don't know what to do with them.
catchers.can: I can digitise them with my field recorder, help you work out whether the singers consented, and point you to the right archive.
catchers.confirm: Were the cassettes recorded in a Shanxi coal town with the singers' knowledge, and do you hold them?

catchers.hypo: I'm a researcher studying song or oral history after industrial closure in another region and would like to compare notes.
catchers.can: I can share how I structure interviews, consent and mapping of who sang to whom, and exchange reading lists.
catchers.confirm: Is your work about how communal singing or oral tradition changes after a workplace or industry closes?

catchers.hypo: I'm a foreigner living in Taiyuan and want to learn real home-style Shanxi noodles from a local cook.
catchers.can: I can ask my neighbour, a retired cook who teaches me knife-cut noodles, whether she'd welcome another student.
catchers.confirm: Are you in Taiyuan now and happy to learn hands-on in a home kitchen, bringing your own appetite?

catchers.hypo: I'm moving to Bergen to study. I'd like to know what daily life, weather and health care are really like there.
catchers.can: I can ask my sister, a nurse in Norway, to share practical advice, and I can describe Bergen myself.
catchers.confirm: Are you planning a move to the Bergen area in the next year and want practical, honest advice?

catchers.hypo: I'm a linguistics grad student working on Shanxi dialect tones and want sung speech as data.
catchers.can: I can ask my Chinese tutor, a linguistics grad student, to talk with you, and with consent we can discuss what field audio could help.
catchers.confirm: Is your research on Shanxi dialect pronunciation or the link between tone and melody?

catchers.hypo: I'm a documentary maker interested in the people left behind when mines close in Shanxi.
catchers.can: I can talk through consent and ethics, and recommend which communities and people might welcome a conversation. I won't share any participant's details without their agreement.
catchers.confirm: Do you want to work slowly and with consent, rather than fast and staged, in places where mines have closed?

catchers.hypo: I'm a graduate student in China or Norway and feel stuck in my fieldwork, with the first approach getting nowhere.
catchers.can: I can share what has and hasn't worked for me, and be a friendly peer who knows the stress of a fixed-length stay.
catchers.confirm: Are you in the middle of fieldwork that isn't going as planned and would like to talk with a peer?

forbids.text: I record only with informed consent and within my ethics approval, and I will not record anyone who hasn't agreed, however useful it would be.
I can pay honoraria only within my fixed research budget, so I can't pay large fees for access.
I will not share participant names, locations or recordings with anyone without their permission.
I'm not looking for stage performances or troupe shows. They are useful elsewhere but not for this project.
My stay in Taiyuan ends in May and my funding is fixed, so I can't take on long-term commitments beyond that.
I can't work in rural dialects without a local interpreter.

projects.name: Coal-town work songs
projects.text: Documenting mining chants, hauling songs and courtship songs from Jincheng, Yangquan, Datong and Zuoquan, with interviews, recordings and a map of who sang to whom and when.

projects.name: Elder-singer archive
projects.text: An archive of consented recordings of elderly singers who learned kaihua-diao and related songs in the village before the 1980s, starting in Zuoquan.

policy.t1: With a real sign of interest I'll say where fieldwork hasn't worked, what kind of informant I look for, and that I pay a modest honorarium.
policy.t2: When trust is high and the other side is clear, I'll share my worries about the grant and how homesick I am.
policy.never: I never give participant details or honoraria beyond my stated range, and I don't hand over my raw notes or recordings.
